title: Nuclear Density; Mass Number; Atomic Number
topicTitle: Nuclear density; mass number; atomic number
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — The Atom's ID Card

Two integers — Z and A — identify any nucleus completely. Z fixes the element and its chemistry; A fixes the isotope and its nuclear behaviour. And the pair explains why all nuclear matter packs to the same astonishing density.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts

### 2.1 Atomic number and mass number

- **Atomic number Z:** the number of protons — defines the element and its position in the periodic table; equals the nuclear charge +Ze and, for a neutral atom, the electron count.
- **Mass number A:** the total number of nucleons (protons + neutrons); A = Z + N.
- Notation: $_{Z}^{A}X$ — e.g. $_{92}^{238}U$ has Z = 92, A = 238, N = 146.

### 2.2 Nuclear radius and density

Nuclear radius grows with the cube root of mass number:
$$R = R_0 A^{1/3}, \qquad R_0 ≈ 1.2 \text{ fm} = 1.2\times10^{-15} \text{ m}$$
Nuclear volume $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 \propto A$, and mass ∝ A, so:
$$\rho = \frac{Am_n}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A} = \frac{m_n}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3} ≈ 2\times10^{17} \text{ kg/m}^3 \quad \text{(constant!)}$$
— nuclear matter is incompressible: every nucleus packs nucleons at the same density.

### 2.3 Worked numericals

**Q (NEB-style):** Find the radius of the $_{92}^{238}U$ nucleus.
$$R = 1.2\times10^{-15} \times 238^{1/3} = 1.2\times10^{-15} \times 6.2 ≈ 7.4\times10^{-15} \text{ m} = 7.4 \text{ fm}$$

**Q (NEB-style):** Compare the densities of $_{1}^{1}H$ and $_{92}^{238}U$ nuclei.
Both ≈ 2×10¹⁷ kg/m³ — density is independent of A; only the radius grows.

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topic 105:** Rutherford's discovery motivates R ∝ A^(1/3) from scattering data.
- **To Topic 107:** same Z, different A = isotopes; same A, different Z = isobars.
- **To Topic 109:** A and Z enter the mass-defect formula directly.

## 4. Exam Orientation and Previous Year Questions (NEB)

### 4.1 Verified PYQs from the solved-paper bank

No verified PYQ for this exact topic in the bank. Practise the R = R₀A^(1/3) numericals and the constant-density argument as **NEB-style practice** (2–3m).

### 4.2 Likely question forms

1. Define Z and A with an example (2m).
2. Show nuclear density is independent of A (3m).
3. Radius numerical for a named nucleus (2–3m).

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Using R ∝ A instead of R ∝ A^(1/3).
2. Confusing Z (protons) with A (nucleons).
3. Forgetting fm = 10⁻¹⁵ m in radius calculations.
specificConditions: Constant Nuclear Density: The result ρ ≈ constant applies to all nuclei (light and heavy) — strong evidence that nuclear force saturates and nucleons are tightly packed.
Approximate Radius Formula: R = R₀A^(1/3) is empirical, valid for A > ~10. Very light nuclei show deviations.
Atomic Mass Unit: 1 u = 1.6605 × 10⁻²⁷ kg = 931.5 MeV/c². Carbon-12 defined as exactly 12 u.

importantStatements: "The mass number A equals the number of protons plus neutrons; the atomic number Z equals the number of protons."

examNotes: Show the density derivation in two lines: mass ∝ A, volume ∝ A.

**Radius grows as A^(1/3), not A** — that cube root is why density stays constant.

summary: Every nucleus is labelled by **atomic number Z** (protons — fixes the element and chemistry) and **mass number A** (protons + neutrons; A = Z + N), written $_{Z}^{A}X$ (uranium-238: Z = 92, N = 146). Scattering data show the radius grows as $R = 1.2A^{1/3}$ fm, so volume ∝ A while mass ∝ A — hence **nuclear density ≈ 2×10¹⁷ kg/m³ is the same for every nucleus**: nuclear matter is effectively incompressible. A uranium nucleus (R ≈ 7.4 fm) and a carbon nucleus (R ≈ 2.7 fm) differ in size, not in density.
